subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF DEALING WITH APPLICATIONS FOR BAIL

speechtext: Mr. FINLAY MacDONALD (Cape Breton South) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 46, to amend the Criminal Code (Bail).

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF DEALING WITH APPLICATIONS FOR BAIL
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF DEALING WITH APPLICATIONS FOR BAIL
speechtext:
This bill is intended to repeal the section of the criminal code dealing with the granting of bail to convicted persons. Under the present arrangement, when a person is convicted only the chief justice or some judge designated by him may grant bail. This is very inconvenient for lawyers practising in the country, because the chief justice usually resides at the provincial capital. This amendment is designated to give any trial judge the right to grant bail to a convicted prisoner, if he thinks fit, until his appeal has been heard. As a matter of fact I know of cases where bail has been refused and the prisoner has remained in gaol for two or three months until his appeal was heard. Then, on the hearing of the appeal, the conviction has been quashed. This amendment is designed to do away with that situation and to enable any trial judge to give bail, under proper circumstances, pending the hearing of the appeal.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: REPORT OF COMMISSIONER RESPECTING ARMENIAN CLAIMS

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
subtopic: REPORT OF COMMISSIONER RESPECTING ARMENIAN CLAIMS
speechtext:
I desire to lay on the table of the house a report made to His Excellency the Governor General in council by Errol M. McDougall, ICC., commissioner on reparations, dealing specially with Armenian claims. If the house would permit it, and at the request of hon. members on both sides, I should like to make a very brief statement as to the purport of the findings of the commissioner.
These claims arise out of the Armenian massacres in 1915, when the Armenian population of Turkey, which was then estimated at
1.800.000,	was two-thirds wiped out, one-third by death and one-third by deportation and dispersal in other countries. Apparently one-third survived, dispersed throughout Turkey. There are a number of Armenians who are naturalized British subjects residing in Canada, and who therefore came within the definition of Canadian nationals within the terms of the treaty of Versailles. The commissioner on reparations has disallowed these claims, to the number of some 270, on three grounds, which may be briefly summarized as follows: First, the property destroyed in Armenia as to the majority of claims, was, according to his findings, the property of Armenians who were Turkish nationals at the time of such destruction, and not the property of their relatives who were then resident in Canada who have proved that they were Canadian nationals at that time. This conclusion rests upon the facts disclosed by the Bryce report and by the findings of the Canadian commissioner, that the destruction of the property took place concurrently with or before tihe massacre of the Armenians, to the number of
600.000.
There occurred, in fact or constructively, a seizure of the property by the Turks before the claimants resident in Canada inherited the property from their relatives then resident in Armenian Turkey. The commissioner therefore finds that the claims of the Canadian claimants did not fall within sections 231 and 232 of part 8, and the annex thereto, of the treaty of Versailles.
The second ground is that by an international convention of November 23, 1923, an international commission was set up at Paris, La Commission Devaluation des Dom-mages subis en Turquie, whioh is known generally as the Paris commission of 1923.
These claimants filed their claims with the Canadian custodian during the term of the late government, and their claims were by that government, through the Canadian custodian of that date, referred to the international commission sitting at Paris. The claimants appeared by counsel before the Paris commission, submitted to that jurisdiction, and put their cases before the commission, offering evidence both documentary and oral. The Paris commission granted awards to certain Canadian claimants for the loss of wife or children at the time of the massacres, but dismissed the property claims of the Canadian nationals on the ground that there was not sufficient evidence to support those claims. The documentary and oral evidence submitted before the Canadian commissioner. Mr. McDougall, was practically identical with the evidence submitted before the international tribunal at Paris, and therefore the Canadian commissioner has dismissed these property claims on the ground that the claimants were estopped in respect of claims which they had submitted already to the Paris commission whose findings were against them.
The third ground is that even although the Canadian commissioner were to assume jurisdiction, the evidence submitted to him, including the evidence submitted before the Paris commission, does not constitute proof of the claims preferred and cannot form the foundation for awards by the Canadian commissioner. In other words, the bulk of the claims made by the Canadian nationals, that is by Armenians who were naturalized British subjects and resident in Canada, were not valid because there was no legal title vested in them prior to or at the time the massacres took place, and when the destruction of property occurred, but their claims were based on title by inheritance to property which would only vest in them upon the death of their compatriots and relatives who were massacred in Turkey; and the commissioner holds that at the time of its destruction the property was vested in Turkish nationals-Armenians then resident in Turkey-and not vested in the Canadian nationals who would have inherited by reason of the death of their relatives by massacre. There was no proof of title nor proof that individual Canadian claimants became exclusively entitled to inherit. Some
600.000	Armenians survived and became dis-

Reparations-Armenian Claims
persed, and there was no proof available to show that even in respect of title by inheritance these Canadian nationals would necessarily have exclusively inherited the property. The commissioner finds also that there is an utter lack of concrete, conclusive evidence as to the value of any property alleged to have been destroped.
These are the general grounds upon which Commissioner McDougall disallowed the 270 Armenian claims. A large number of the hon. members are interested in this matter and I am told that it is likely to be brought up again for discussion.
By leave of the house, I beg to move, seconded by the right hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley):
That four hundred copies in the English language and two hundred copies in the French language of the special report by Errol M. McDougall, K.C., Commissioner on Reparation, upon Armenian claims laid on the table of the house this day be printed forthwith and that standing order 64 in relation thereto be suspended.

Mr. MAURICE BRASSET (Gaspe) moved the first reading of Bill No. 42, to amend the Bankruptcy Act as respects locality of a debtor.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, this bill has reference to the province of Quebec and would require a petition to be filed in the judicial district wherein the debtor resides, such district to be as defined by the Quebec statutes. This bill would lessen the expenses of insolvents. For instance, at the present time the courts in Hull or in Montreal may accept a petition to declare insolvent a resident of Gaspe county, and that person is obliged to come to Hull or to Montreal in order to defend the petition. The purpose of this bill is to obviate that trouble and expense.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
There was a question before the committee in regard to certain transactions by the board of grain supervisors, and by t'he wheat board, in the years 1917, 1918 and 1919. This question arose out of certain letters which passed between a gentleman named Whiteside and the minister of the day, Sir George Foster. As a matter of fact, the more one searches and looks into this matter at this late date, Ithe more one is puzzled to . know just why the matter has been stirred up in the way it has, because it must be clear to members of the committee that it is very difficult for the officers of the department, thirteen or fourteen years after the events have happened, and it having been assumed for the last ten years that the matter was closed and ended, to place their fingers on all the records, particularly when those records were very largely in the hands of the two boards.
However, I have here a statement regarding the board of grain supervisors, audited by George A. Touche & Company, which shows that the business of the board was very properly handled and all the funds accounted for. Such amount as may have been left, and the records of the board, were handed over to the wheat board which followed. Then 22X10-1011
in turn the wheat board completed its business in 1921 and there was printed and supplied by order of parliament in that year, although I have not the exact date, a complete report of the wheat board, with financial statement. This brought the matter to a finality, and showed a certain sum, approximately half a million dollars, left in the consolidated revenue fund. Under order in council the government which preceded this government paid out to the western provinces 8560,000.
And to the eastern provinces as well.

Yes, to all the provinces. I have the figures here. The order in council is P.C. 193, dated 7th February, 1925, and the moneys were paid out as follows:
Saskatchewan	 $284,200
Manitoba	 128,800
Alberta	 112,000
Ontario	 26,600
Quebec	 6,440
British Columbia	 1,960
This memorandum indicates that a further sum of $175,000 was sent to the Department of Finance and is still in hand, less a small amount which was deducted for certain expenses, leaving a net amount of $173,235.53. Very briefly that is the outcome of these transactions.

Before the minister leaves those figures I should like to ask a question. He said there was some amount transferred by the board, which was in charge in 1917 and 1918, to the wheat board in 1919. Can he tell us how much that -was?
There was remitted to the receiver general at that time $428,781.94. That was the cash in hand, but the records and books and the other paraphernalia were turned over to the wheat board.
No money was turned over to the wheat board?
No. I notice there was a small item of about $500 paid to the Royal Bank of Canada at Winnipeg, which was a small amount held against some local account.
So that $428,000 was actually the proceeds of the transactions that had been carried on with those two crops?
Yes.

Then I should like to ask the minister, in view of the fact that
8428,000	was turned over from the operations of the 1917-18 crop by the wheat supervisors, what was meant by the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) when he stated there was no profit made?

Supply-Canada Grain Act

I think I can very easily explain that to my hon. friend. Certain very small charges were made by the board of grain supervisors for the handling and storage of the grain. They had a revenue, according to this statement, which arose from a small assessment on all grain which was exported, and which was used to cover their expenditures, amounting to S7,302,000. That was the revenue from the handling of 350,000,000 bushels of wheat. Then they had a domestic assessment of 83,017,420, or a total income of $10,320,161.06 under that head. This, of course, was spent in carrying charges for street wheat and for wheat held by or for flour mills. The amount expended in this way was $7,211,112.77. The Department of Agriculture seed grain purchasing committee received $146,000, and there were ordinary disbursements and expenses.
The administration expenses were very small. I commend these figures to the attention of the house, as they are about as good a guarantee as could be secured of the manner in which the business was done. Administration expenses amounted to $183,727.37, No salaries were paid to the members of the board, but wages were paid to employees, clerks and so on. The board secured their offices from the Winnipeg grain exchange, and paid nothing for rental as far as the head office was concerned. Travelling expenses amounted to about 825,000; there were rentals outside of head office; telephones and telegrams amounted to S6.000, and so on. A number of miscellaneous small expenses make a total of $183,000, so that is an indication of a very moderate expenditure in that regard. After all this work was done there remained the sum to which I have referred, which was landed to the receiver general.
Now I should like to make just a brief statement with regard to a report from Doctor Magill which we have succeeded in finding, made in March, 1920, with regard to the board of grain supervisors. Perhaps before I refer to that I should draw attention to a condition which obtained in 1916-17. In 1916 there was a large crop, and there was a considerable amount of tough grain which it was very difficult to market. I think I am right in saying it was the winter of 1916 and 1917. And when the overseas purchasing countries were drawing their usual purchases of high grade Nos. 1, 2 and 3, there, was a shortage of these grades for their purposes. There was a tendency for the market to be cornered. But there was in Canada a very large quantity of this tough or off-grade grain. It was in connection with that particular work, I believe, that the hon. member for South Winnipeg, 
who was then a member of the government, rendered such excellent service while in the old country. I think it was largely through his efforts that satisfactory arrangements were made with the overseas purchasing countries to take this grain off our hands. I recall, as
1	believe he will bear me out, that some of the purchasers over there-and, mark you, at this time they were largely government purchasers, later on solely such

were afraid to risk the transportation of this damp or tough grain to the old country under war conditions, and naturally they were looking for the usual high grade wheat from Canada. After negotiations by the Canadian government they undertook to take this wheat off our hands, and they did take it at an excellent price to the producers.
What was the price?
The price was around $2 a bushel.
But what was the price paid by the purchasing commission on the other side? Was it not $2.21 plus cost of delivery in United Kingdom?

The prices varied. I have here a statement prepared by the bureau of statistics, showing the average price of wheat in Chicago and in Winnipeg. I shall give these statements in detail to Hansard, and in the meantime, if the committee so desires, I will quote a few figures. For No. 1 Manitoba northern the average price in 1917, Fort William and Port Arthur basis, was 220-5. In Chicago the average for that year was 2-278. In 1918 the average in Winnipeg was 222-1 and in Chicago 2-209. In 1919 the average in Winnipeg was 221-0 and in Chicago 2-35- 2-39.
That is 1918, is it not?
That is 1919.
In 1919 it was under the old wheat board, you know.
Of course, it was a fixed price in both countries. These are the figures that have been given. In 1919 there was a free market in Chicago.
And in Canada.
But in regard to this last figure it must be recalled that, as mentioned the other day, there was a second distribution which brought the Canadian price up to 2-63 or 2-64. That is about correct.

The minister has
given us everything except what we want. What we wish to know is how much wheat was sold those two years and what it brought in the British market. That is really the crux of the whole matter.

The amount sold was
350,000,000 bushels.
That is about right, for the two years.

find. The settling of the purchases was made by the British government, through the Wheat Export Company, a public body. Settlement was made direot, through the usual channels, with the farmers here, who got the full amount, whatever it was, less the small assessment which was made. The assessed amount was the only sum handled by the board of grain supervisors. Does that clear the matter up?

My hon. friend is not.
doing justice either to himself or to myself.
Possibly not.

I would ask the committee to note this. I have avoided anything in the nature of the tu quoque argument; I have

not asked, "Why didn't you do it"? May I call attention to the fact that from the close of the operations of the wheat board in 1920 -their report was presented in 1921-down to nine months ago, my hon. friend was a member of the government in office during that period-the government that had all these things in their custody.

We had not any
complaint except 1919.

The information in connection with forty-five cases was found to have been stored by the government of which my hon. friend was a member in a building down on Wellington street. As fas ns I know, every scrap of paper which was used by the two boards is there. Surely it is not suggested that we, because of absolutely unsupported suggestions-
They are not unsupported.

If my hon. friend will pardon me-unsupported suggestions should reopen this whole question and spend an unknown amount in the reexamination of these transactions. If any hon. member or other responsible person will come forward and say that of his own knowledge there are grounds for suspicion that everything is not correct, then parliament would be justified in considering the reopening of this question and having all the documents examined. The committee should not forget that I have here the report of the board of grain supervisors and the auditor's statement of the amount handled by the whole system, which was a system of control in all parts of the world. No dissatisfaction was expressed; as a matter of fact those few years were the most prosperous years we have ever experienced, if we eliminate the war period. It is now being suggested that without any evidence being produced this government, my department and my officials should be able to give a complete statement of the transactions of these two boards operating in western Canada with headquarters in Winnipeg. Let me read briefly from the. report .of the Canadian wheat board, season 1020.
That is the wheat board of 1910?

That is the title upon this parliamentary document, printed by the king's printer by order. of parliament. In this parliamentary record we have a history of the whole business, the transition from one to the other.

Supply-Canada Grain Act
I understand those are the records handed over by the board of grain supervisors to the wheat board of 1919.

It discusses the appointment of the wheat board. It refers to the two years previous wherein the transaction had been carried on under the control of the government and the board of grain supervisors. It discusses the armistice; it deals with the activities of the grain corporation in the United States under Mr. Julius Barnes, and it gives the plan of the organization of the board. There is one heading entitled "A Thorny Path", so I do not imagine it was all a bed of roses. It discusses the relations with the United States, seed grain, prospects for selling crops, the course of the world's demand, the decontrol of flour, the payment of dividends on participating certificates, the question of spread, branch offices of the board, and so on. At the end of the report is the financial statement which indicates the expenses of the board. This statement does not give all the figures, that is, the total amount received and paid out, but it does show that there was a balance of some $65,000,000, which amount was dispersed under regulations 1*1)9 and 127 at the rate of 48 cents per bushel on 135,000,000 bushels.

That is the balance from
the wheat board?

I am speaking of the
wheat board.

We are agreed on that.
I would point out that the minister is bringing forth new evidence, and I would again submit that because of that new evidence this whole thing should be referred to the committee on agriculture. This matter could be cleared up more easily in that way. We do not desire to take up the time of the committee in discussing this matter.

Why does not the hon.
member tell us what is in his mind?

I will tell the hon.
member in a moment.

It seems to me it would be easier, both for the minister and for his department, to handle this matter in the way suggested. I cannot understand why the minister can produce a report submitted by the grain supervisors which gives' the volume but does not give a financial statement. He has been able to obtain that report; possibly he could obtain the financial statement from the same source.

Mr. Chairman, there seems to be a suspicion in western Canada that a certain fund was left over, and I would like to answer the hon. member for South Battle-ford (Mr. Vallance) in that regard. The farmers of western Canada individually, and not the government received that $2.21 per bushel. As was pointed out by the hon. member for South Winnipeg, each farmer received about $2.21 at his station.

We all agree on
that.

The hon. member for
South Winnipeg stated that the farmer got everything which was paid for the wheat.
So he did.

Where did the surplus
come from that is mentioned by the minister?

With a volume running
into hundreds of millions of bushels there will always be a surplus, and there was a surplus.
We agree on that.

The suspicion as outlined
by Mr. Whiteside is that instead of the government selling this wheat at $2.21 less an expenditure for handling, it was sold at around S3 per bushel, which created a surplus of millions of dollars.

The Hon. Sir George
Foster stated:
The wheat was sold during the season of 1917 and 1918, as purchasers were found and, of course, for different prices owing to changes in the world's market price.

That was on the basis
of $2.21 for No. 1 northern; the lower grades would be at a different price.
It was on the basis of $2.21 for No. 1 northern.

If Mr. Whiteside's contention was right we would have millions of dollars of a surplus, but I do not think any hon. member of the opposition suggests that any such surplus exists. I received for my 1917-18 crop that amount, less a small expenditure, and I think most hon. members will agree with the statement that the farmers of western Canada as a whole received that amount less a small expenditure for handling.

The farmers got
$2.63 in 1919 and the provinces received a
Supply-Canada Grain Act

refund on a pro rata basis from the late government aggregating about half a million dollars, resulting from an operating surplus by the wheat board.

That was in 1919, under
the wheat board. [DOT]

Why should we
not get it now for 1917 and 1918?

Let us get this point clear. We cannot expect, as I have already indicated, to get now for 1917 and 1918 what was paid to us individually. When we marketed our wheat in 1917 and 1918, we got the whole proceeds of that crop, all we expected. Are hon. members not agreed on that?
No.

I think we are agreed on
it. I want to ask this question: If we did not get it, why should we wait twelve or thirteen years to raise the question?
Because we did not know of it until last fall.

Will hon. members not
agree with me that a man named Whiteside sent out a suggestion, let me say-he had no proof-

He had a letter from the
minister.
-that we had millions and millions of dollars in the treasury from the fact that wheat was sold at a profit of fifty or sixty cents a bushel. That is the contention Mr. Whiteside made.

That is the point we
want to clear up.

That is where the whole
suspicion lies in western Canada. Do hon. members not agree with me the suspicion is, as I have said, that the government profiteered on us in 1917?

We want the
government to show they did not.
Are we not agreed to take the explanation?

Let us conduct business in an
orderly fashion. One member at a time should address the chair.

The government could not show in dollars the amount of money involved in the sale of millions and millions of bushels because it never went into the treasury at all; it went to the farmers in 1917 and 1918. The government never handled that money at all.
To whom was it paid?
The money was paid to the farmers of western Canada.
Through what body?
Through the trade. Through whatever elevator the farmer delivered his wheat to. That is one way it was paid at that time.
Was it not paid through the board of grain supervisors?
Not at all.
What did the trade sell the wheat at?

At $2.21, I understand. As far as the individual was concerned, the money was paid to him in western Canada through whatever elevator the wheat was delivered to. If the minister will forget about 1919 and the wheat board and clear up the 1917 and 1918 transactions, the latter is what the dispute is over; there is no dispute over the 1919 crop at all. It is in regard to 1917 and 1918 that this man Whiteside says those profits were made that we did not get.

The problem resolves itself into this: the minister has before him and has already given to the house the total crop value for the years in question. He has also stated that the average price in those years was so much, but of course the minister knows very well the average price for a year does not in any way indicate the price received for the total crop; that would depend upon the quantity sold at various price levels throughout the year.
And the grades.

Yes; and in order to get an accurate picture of the situation, one ought to foe able to place before the committee the total sum received from the wheat. We can -then deduct What the farmers got for the wheat and deduce whether or not there was any profit. Until that is settled, this will remain a cloud over the administration of that time. I submit to the minister that after all the requests are very reasonable; this is not being made a party question at all. All that hon. gentlemen to my right have asked is that the matter be referred to the committee where witnesses may be examined, documents tabled and facts ascertained. I strongly support them in that request. Even my hon. friend who belongs to the minister's own party, and who has just concluded his remarks, considered it fair that we should clear this matter up now. I think it should go to the committee.

Supply-Canada Grain Act

Would the minister clear up this point-it seems to me we are in doubt about it also? Did the board of grain supervisors actually handle the cash for the wheat, or was it handled through the trade -for 1916, 1917 and 1918? Did they receive the money for the wheat and in turn pay it out to the farmers, or was the money handled by the trade, the board of grain supervisors merely supervising the matter and collecting certain handling fees?

As nearly as I can answer that question from the documents, the board of grain supervisors did not handle the money which was paid for the grain in 1917 and 1918. The board of grain supervisors, by a decision of the board, worked through the grain trade. The only sums that the board of grain supervisors handled were the sums to which I have referred and for which I hold in my hand an audited statement by George A. Touc'he & Company. The total amount handled by them was 810,478,000 for which they have accounted in every detail, with an audited statement from George A. Touche & Company Payments were made to the farmers by the trade through the usual channels. In his report Doctor Magill refers to that and says they had before them the option of two courses, if I am not mistaken, and that they adopted the course of working through the trade. Therefore, as far as I can see, the board did not directly handle the funds.

They must have
handled some, when they had nearly half a million in overages, elevator fees, storage.

That was an assessment. Let us get that point clear and then I think we can get nearer to a solution of 'the matter. That was a small assessment they made upon all the grain they handled. Out of the proceeds of that assessment, plus certain earnings they made by investing their surplus holdings in that regard in certain securities, they got a total revenue of $10,478,000. Then they iisbursed that. Most of it was disbursed for carrying charges and then there were certain administrative charges and so forth. That left them with the small amount, comparatively speaking, of $428,781, which was turned over to the receiver general. If my (hon. friend will permit me, may I attempt to make the point clear that out of the handling of that wheat for those two years, the board of grain supervisors had $428,781 left. It was that, plus a small surplus from the wheat board, which constituted what was remaining in the hands of the government. The government
in 1925-and -my hon. friend was a member of -the then government-disbursed that to the provinces in part, leaving still in the treasury $173,000.
For possible outstanding claims.

There were no other funds left with the government than this. The records are, I think, clear on that point, unless hon. gentlemen go to the extent, which I do not think is reasonable, of having a reaudit of all the transactions of t-he board of grain supervisors and the wheat board. That I think all would agree would be a very foolish thing in the face of the evidence that we have before us, which I think is quite convincing that the matter was handled properly and effectively.

There is one point that
does not seem quite clear. We are told that all the money that the board of grain supervisors handled was that ten million dollars, but it has not been shown to the house yet who handled the money that was received from the sale of those 350,000,000 bushels. Who received that money when that wheat was sold?

Who sold the wheat?
That is the first question that should be answered.
One at a time, please.
Then I will go on. Was the board of grain supervisors responsible for selling the wheat, and for making the bargains? They bought our wheat in those two years, 1917 and 1918.

I suppose if I read a few pages of this file I could make it clearer, but will hon. gentlemen take my word for it when I summarize in this way.
The board of grain supervisors, acting for the government of the day in Canada, in collaboration with the government of Great Britain and other countries purchasing through them, arranged for the sale of the wheat, but the actual transaction, that is, the passing of the money to the farmers from the wheat export board, which represented the British government in Canada and the United States, was done through the regular channels, that is, through the elevator companies, and so forth. In the meantime the trading in futures on the Winnipeg grain exchange was shut down. The elevator companies, however, were still operating in the normal way, and the report
Supply-Canada Grain Act

shows that they cooperated very satisfactorily in this respect with the board of grain supervisors.
Let me repeat: The board of grain supervisors did not handle the money. They made the arrangements officially, representing the producers or vendors on this side, with the governments of the purchasing countries on the other side. The governments of the purchasing countries bought through the wheat exporting company, and they paid the farmers through the regular channels, namely, through the grain elevator companies and the grain handling companies of Canada. I wonder if that is clear.

There is a point that is
not clear yet. It is true that the farmer received that price of $2.21 a bushel. There was no question of our getting more out of it at that time, no thought of its being an initial or an interim payment. We received that money. Now somebody took charge of that wheat and sold it on the markets of the world, and the amount sold is stated at 350,000,000 bushels. We are told that that was handled by a grain exporting company. If they sold that wheat, according to the letter of Sir George Foster, at the market prices that prevailed from time to time, the proceeds from the sale of that wheat came to them, and no accounting of that money has since been given to anybody. It is true that we sold that wheat as farmers and took the price of $2.21 a bushel, and were given no reason to expect we were going to get any more, but we did think that when the government guaranteed us a price of $2.21, that, wheat was going to the allies at that price, plus whatever handling expenses were necessary. That was our understanding of the matter. It now appears that that was not exactly what happened.
Oh yes.

No, it is not, because according to the letter of Sir George Foster, the wheat was sold on the markets of the world at varying prices from time to time. There was an amount of 350,000,000 bushels sold, and we have no record of what was received for that wheat by the body that was handling the sale of it for the farmers of Canada.
I think that we are getting aearer to an understanding. My hon. friend has made one mistake. He said that the board of grain supervisors undertook to sell the wheat.

No. I accept the minister's statement as to that.
[Mr. Stevens.1

My hon. friend used that phrase, and I think that is 'where confusion is being caused in the minds of some. Let me read an extract from the report of Dr. Magill, which I think will at least assist in clearing up that point. He says:
For the crop year of 1917 there was no difficulty in this respect. The allies needed the whole exportable surplus wheat of Canada. They were willing to buy the whole surplus at the price fixed-
Which was $2.21, I think.
-and they gave a guarantee to that effect. In this respect wheat was in a different position from coarse grains.
That is 1917. Let us stop there for a moment. The allies, all of them, I imagine, represented through the wheat exporting company, undertook to take all our wheat and to pay a fixed price. Now what was the duty of Canada? One only, and that was to provide the mechanical means of getting that wheat to the allies. What did we do in that respect? We used all the existing machinery; physically, the elevators; from the financial point of view, the banks and the grain companies. The grain companies handled it just the same as they had done in any other year, but instead of going to the farmers in various localities and offering them a price, they paid a fixed price to all and that was the end of it, and the farmer got the full amount. The money was paid to him as he delivered his wheat at the station or at the car. That ended the transaction so far as Canada was concerned. The board bf grain supervisors never touched the money. I again quote from the report of Dr. Magill:
It was different with the crop of 1918. No guarantee was obtained from tbe representatives of the British royal commission with regard to the surplus of the crop of 1918, and when the armistice was signed there was considerable difficulty in selling the balance of wheat still remaining in Canada. Having, however, fixed a price tor the wheat of 1918, and having arranged for the purchase of wheat from the farmer by the trade on that basis, a guarantee was necessary and it was given by the Dominion government.
That was in the year 1918. That guarantee was given in the absence of a guarantee by the British or allied governments, or the wheat exporting company. The Canadian government guaranteed that that price would be continued through the season to the farmer, and that was done. The report continues :	.
Fortunately the allied countries needed the wheat, and in the end the balance of the crop of 1918 was sold at the fixed price.

Supply-Canada Grain Act
That was the end of the activities of the Canadian government through the board of grain supervisors, so far as those two years are concerned. If there is any clearer way in which I can give it, I shall be glad to do so.

What the minister has
said was done, is exactly what we thought was being done; I say that frankly. But it does not seem to harmonize with the statements upon which Mr. Whiteside acted. He understood from Sir George Foster that the wheat was sold at varying prices from time to time. There is that conflict of statement.
Suppose we look at Mr. Whiteside's letter again.

So far as Mr. Whiteside
personally is concerned, I never heard of him till I got down here at the beginning of the session.

I do not think my hon.
friends really wish to embarrass the government in this matter.

No, we want to get the
facts; that is all.

May I ask them in all
fairness this question? I do not wish to reflect on Mr. W'hiteside at all. He is a citizen of this country and, as Sir George Foster frequently states in his painstaking reply, he takes him to be an honest citizen looking for information. 'Sir George Foster, I repeat, painstakingly answered him, and anyone who peruses these letters will find the complete answer in the letters themselves, I am sure, because Mr. Whiteside deals with nothing but rumours or conjectures that are in his own mind.
No, no.

If I am wrong, I wish my hon. friend to correct me. But as I understand it, the policy called' Canada first means " adequate protection". It does not mean having at heart the interests of Canada or anything of that sort. As a slogan it is Canada first, and as an economic or fiscal policy it is a concrete proposal or principle synonomous with a system of adequate protection. Am I wrong in that? My hon. friend does not reply, and I assume his silence signifies assent. Adequate protection, then, is what is intended. The Prime Minister has said, "We will be the judge of what is adequate protection; and we intend, in judging what constitutes adequate protection, that nothing shall come into this country from abroad which can be produced or manufactured in Canada." Again I pause to have my hon. friend correct me if I am wrong. The Prime Minister goes further and says, "We want to trade with other parts of the empire, but we will not begin until we have attained for Canada the ends of adequate protection

at which we aim; and if other parts of the empire wish to trade with us they must follow our example in the matter of creating protective tariffs. And we will increase by ten per cent, or whatever percentage is necessary, the duties against foreign countries to make it still more difficult for trade to come in from foreign countries; such trade as on a reciprocal basis thus established can flow in from within the empire may come in." That policy means a serious restriction of trade, and the country to-day is beginning to feel the very serious effects of it. Mr. MoMILLAN (Huron) : This discussion has been very interesting to me and I have been indeed pleased to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has acquitted himself admirably in his very difficult situation. When he was explaining recently his conception of the trade policy of the present government, I happened to open Hansard of last September and I saw that the Prime Minister told us then very explicitly what the policy of this government was in that respect. He said:
We propose therefore to provide that so far as may be reasonably possible the requirements of the 10,000,000 people living on the northern half of this continent shall be provided by Canadian producers.
There is no equivocation in connection with that policy. Anyone who can read plain English ought to know what it means. It means that he is going to exclude from Canada any goods that we are capable of producing in this country. In other words, they are going to try to sell goods to the world, without buying goods in return. Now, surely it is an economic principle which every reasonable individual should appreciate, that if we are going to sell goods we must be prepared to buy goods in return.
I think the statement which was made by the Prince of Wales at the opening of the exhibition at Buenos Aires was one from which we might learn a lesson. That statement is instructive to people in all sections of the British Empire and throughout the world at large. His Royal Highness said that the real objects of trade, the purpose of trade was the interchange of products. I do not need to tell this house a second time that I do not believe that the representatives of this government met with any degree of success in their mission to the old countiy when
they attended the Imperial conference last fall. It is my candid opinion that the chief reason for their abject failure was that the Prime Minister and his colleagues seemed to have been convinced that we should not import from abroad goods which we can produce at home, and that the very idea of allowing Canadian industry to meet with competition was unacceptable to them. They did not believe that competition should be encouraged.
Now, Mr. Chairman, my experience in life in every particular convinces me that the spirit of competition, the spirit of healthy emulation, is the best thing for any nation or individual, if you wish to bring out the best that is in them. We see, on the other hand, what the policy of the present government is; and that policy being what it is, what is the use of spending 1700,000 on trade missions to other countries? What is the use of such an expenditure when evidently the government does not wish to encourage reciprocal trade?
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer. The Prime Minister and his colleagues went to Great Britain, to attend the Imperial conference. The Minister of Trade and Commerce took a number of wideawake officials with him, and we know they have broken down the entire sales service of the wheat pool. They have thrown the selling of wheat right into the hands of those who for years have been the determined competitors of the pool. If that is the best thing to do in the selling of our wheat, then I fail to see how the wheat pool is going to be able to pursue its business in the future as it has done, in the past. I am not one of those who think that the wheat pool, those who had in hand the sale of our wheat, have never made mistakes. Nevertheless, I do think that the government is mistaken in its attitude. So far as western Canada is concerned, we know what has been the result of the establishment of the wheat pool and the work which they have done in the last few years. We know what was the situation of the grain growers in the west when they were at the mercy of the grain trade, and I cannot see how the action of the government in withdrawing the sales force which we have had, and placing the whole business of the grain trade in the hands of their competitors, will be of any benefit to the wheat pool in the west.
